input_classification: Synthetic educational Python game request; the model response is a real provider result.

rubric.evidence: k1 explicitly targets Python; k2-k6 explicitly target pygame. The technical plan correctly says Python was requested and only the graphics library was unspecified; pygame is clearly a modifiable assumption. No unit copies a whole project stack. This verifies proposed retrieval targets, not any video's actual coverage.

f1/k2 covers the local window, rendering and quit handling; f2/k3 covers held left/right keys and bounds; f3/k4-k5 covers falling, collision, score and respawn; f4/k6 covers a missed ball and the final score; f5/k6 covers in-game Space restart. Scope retains no login or network requirement.

Six units form buildable steps. k1 combines variables, numeric types, updates and printed inspection in a concrete script holding paddle/ball coordinates and score; this is a limited prerequisite practice, not an isolated variable name or one-line syntax lesson. The remaining units teach event/render loop, visible movement, collision, score/respawn and end/restart state behavior.

k1 numerical state precedes k2 window/event loop; k3 movement follows the loop; k4 falling/collision follows drawing and movement; k5 score/respawn follows collision; k6 final state/reset follows those data paths. The serial order is conservative but coherent for a beginner. while/if and running scripts are explicit adjustable assumptions rather than established learner facts.

rubric.criterion: No unrelated features or broad-subject substitutes
rubric.evidence: The proposal adds no account, leaderboard, network, database, cloud deployment or unrelated course. Constant falling speed, plus-one scoring and local scripts are scoped assumptions. Python fundamentals do not replace the five actual pygame project units.

rubric.criterion: Technical consistency of game-over and restart
rubric.evidence: The technical plan says to pause only physics/scoring while events and the game-over screen continue. f4 stops falling/scoring, not the main loop; f5 explicitly says the main loop never exited. k6 consistently uses a state flag and Space KEYDOWN to reset score/positions and restore play. The observed v5 stop-the-game-loop contradiction is absent.

Checks are practical: inspect changed numbers, open/close a window, hold a direction at an edge, trigger a catch, see plus-one score/respawn, then miss and restart. beginner is retained; adjustment_note explicitly says zero project experience and invites changing stage or selections. The path assumes basic while/if and script execution, so it does not claim a fully zero-code introductory course.

unit_review.task: A numeric game-state script updates coordinates and score and prints the before/after values.
Build a refreshed blank window with a running event loop and working QUIT handling.
Draw a paddle, move it with held keys and clamp it to the screen.
Animate the ball and detect its Rect overlapping the paddle; a simple collision approximation is appropriate to this beginner scope.
Add one point per catch, render the score and move the caught ball back to the top.
Pause playing updates on a miss while preserving the live event/render loop, then reset the data on Space.

low_priority_teaching_notes.observation: The chosen simplification uses a fixed displacement per frame, but the loop unit does not explicitly include a frame-rate cap or elapsed-time scaling.
low_priority_teaching_notes.recommended_follow_up: When building or reviewing the student's executable game, include a Clock.tick frame cap or elapsed-time movement and test behavior on the actual machine.
low_priority_teaching_notes.why_not_blocking_this_analysis: The artifact is a learning-needs proposal with no executable game or cross-machine timing promise; all requested behaviors have coherent units. This note must not be treated as execution verification.
